content:
[31-degree WBGT index is "dangerous"]

[Hong Kong has yet to establish warning levels based on the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index. However, according to Japan's Ministry of the Environment website, a WBGT above 28 is classified as "high alert," during which strenuous exercise or activities like long-distance running that easily raise body temperature should be avoided, and those with weaker physique or who are not acclimated to hot environments should stop exercising; a WBGT above 31 is already classified as "dangerous," and exercise should be halted except in special circumstances. Singapore's National Environment Agency also classifies a WBGT of 33 degrees or above as "high heat stress," advising the public to minimise outdoor activities and stay in shaded areas.]

[Reviewing last week's data: WBGT exceeded 32 degrees at nine of ten stations on 8.8]

[The Hong Kong Observatory provided "集誌社" with the highest 60-minute average WBGT readings recorded at monitoring stations from August 3 to 9. The data shows that on August 7 and 9——last Friday and this Sunday——nine of the ten monitoring stations recorded readings exceeding 32 degrees at some point. On Saturday, August 8, all ten monitoring stations recorded readings above 32 degrees, with four stations recording WBGT above 34 degrees. The Wetland Park monitoring station recorded the highest readings of the week, reaching 35 and 34.8 degrees on Saturday and Sunday respectively.]

[As for the record-breaking heat on August 9, the highest WBGT recorded at Observatory monitoring stations was 33.5 degrees, but the "Hong Kong Heat Index" that day remained below 32, so only a yellow work heat stress warning was issued. Lam Chiu-ying explained that in the WBGT formula, "globe temperature" reflecting sun exposure accounts for 20%, while in the Hong Kong Heat Index formula, "globe temperature" only accounts for 5%, making the index necessarily lower than WBGT and unable to reflect the hardships faced by outdoor workers.]

[Lam Chiu-ying: Even August 8 should have been a black warning]

[Lam said the WBGT readings reflected that outdoor workers experienced "even greater hardship" on August 8. From last Friday to Sunday, multiple monitoring stations recorded WBGT exceeding 33 degrees, which by international standards falls within the "dangerous" category. He believed at least a red warning should have been issued, quipping: "It depends on whether you love your people or not. If you love your people, even August 8 should have been a black warning."]

[Hong Kong should follow Japan's example and establish a reporting mechanism]

[Japan's authorities amended regulations last year, stipulating that in workplaces where WBGT reaches 28 degrees or above, or where air temperature reaches 31 degrees or above, working continuously for more than one hour or accumulating four hours within a day would be considered work with heatstroke risk. Employers must establish heatstroke reporting mechanisms for employees and implement measures to prevent heatstroke from worsening, including allowing employees to leave the site when necessary. Employers who violate the rules face a maximum sentence of six months' imprisonment or a fine of 500,000 yen. Lam Chiu-ying lamented that under the current system, even if outdoor workers suffer heatstroke during work, it is difficult to obtain evidence for work injury compensation. He believes Hong Kong should also follow Japan in establishing a reporting mechanism.]

[Commissioner for Labour Hui Tak-sun said yesterday that the authorities would review the mechanism. Lam Chiu-ying urged the authorities to make greater reference to the WBGT index and the implementation practices of other countries, and to discuss with the Hong Kong Observatory how to put this into effect. In the interim, they could borrow from the Mainland's "Measures for the Administration of Heatstroke Prevention and Cooling," which uses maximum temperatures of 35, 37 and 40 degrees as thresholds for yellow, red and black work heat stress warnings, to avoid the embarrassment of "not seeing red even when records are broken," and to avoid causing public anxiety.]
